findings.summary: Localhost OAuth callback accepts any `code` with no CLI-generated nonce/state binding (pre-existing, outside the diff) — login-confusion / session fixation
findings.evidence: `startCallbackServer` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:168-182) serves 127.0.0.1/callback and resolves on the first `code` query param it sees, with no check that the code corresponds to the OAuth flow this process started: no CLI-generated nonce is embedded in the `?mode=cli&port=` URL (line 36) and none is verified on the callback, and there is no Origin/Sec-Fetch check. The code is then exchanged unconditionally at line 56 and the resulting tokens persisted at line 138. Attack: while a victim runs `wafflebase login` (a 30s window, line 237), an attacker who has obtained a valid CLI code for their OWN account gets the victim's browser to issue `GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker-code>` (img/fetch; the opaque response does not matter) and races the legitimate callback across the ephemeral port range. If the attacker's code lands first, the victim's CLI session is fixed to the attacker's account and subsequent `files upload` / `docs import` operations write the victim's data into the attacker's workspace. I could not confirm the port-guessing race is practical in the wild, hence low confidence; this code predates the diff and I cite it because the login action has no try/catch and therefore lands in the `runCli` catch this change modified.

findings.summary: Nonce-mismatch coverage only exercises the length-differs branch, so a length-only comparison would pass
findings.evidence: `nonceMatches` (login.ts:164-169) is `a.length === b.length && timingSafeEqual(a, b)`. The test's two rejection cases are no state at all and `state=guessed` (7 chars) against `the-nonce` (9 chars) — both short-circuit on the length check, so `timingSafeEqual` is never reached with a mismatching same-length value. Replacing the body with `return a.length === b.length` (accepting any 9-char attacker state) leaves the suite green. A same-length wrong-value case (e.g. `state=xxx-nonce`) is what would pin the actual comparison.

findings.summary: The new CLI login `nonce` is a bearer-grade binding secret carried in a URL query string that the request logger records verbatim (redaction covers headers only)
findings.evidence: `packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:46` sends the secret as a query param: `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}&nonce=${encodeURIComponent(nonce)}`. On the backend, pino-http's request serializer logs `url: req.url` (`app.module.ts:68`) — the full path *with* query string — and the `redact.paths` list (`app.module.ts:76-83`) only censors `req.headers.authorization`, `req.headers.cookie` and `res.headers["set-cookie"]`; nothing strips query parameters. `customLogLevel` maps this 302 GET to `debug`, so it is silent at default `info`, but any deployment with `LOG_LEVEL=debug`, any 4xx on that route (→ `warn`, logged at info), or any reverse proxy / CDN access log in front of the backend captures the nonce together with the callback port, both in the same line. Attack: read one log line, then from any page in the victim's browser navigate to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker-code>&state=<leaked-nonce>` inside the 30s window (`login.ts:257-265`) — `nonceMatches` at `login.ts:206` passes and the CLI redeems the attacker's code, which is precisely the RFC 8252 §8.9 outcome the change claims to prevent. The whole mitigation collapses to the secrecy of a query parameter that the repo logs unredacted.

mergedFrom.summary: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` has no proof-of-possession: the nonce now available server-side is not required to redeem the code

findings.summary: CLI auth code is still not bound to the client (no PKCE); the nonce only gates the local listener, so an intercepted code is fully redeemable
findings.evidence: The change cites RFC 8252 §8.9, whose actual prescription for the loopback-redirect code-injection problem is PKCE. What landed is a `state` echo checked only inside the CLI's own listener (`packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:206`). The code itself remains an unbound bearer: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (auth.controller.ts:152-168) takes `{ code }` with no authentication, no `code_verifier`, and no reference to the nonce — `consumeCode` looks up only the code (cli-auth.store.ts:71). Attack: anyone who observes the code within its 60s TTL — from the victim's browser history/URL bar (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…` is a real navigation), a browser extension, a shared/kiosk machine, or an intercepting proxy — POSTs it to /auth/cli/exchange and receives the victim's `accessToken` + `refreshToken`. The nonce does nothing here because the CLI listener is not in the path. Grepped the whole repo for pkce/code_verifier/code_challenge: zero hits. Severity is 'major' rather than 'critical' because it needs code interception, and confidence is low because I could not demonstrate a concrete interception channel in this codebase.

findings.summary: Login callback server again redeems the first `code` that hits the loopback port, with no binding to the flow this process started
findings.evidence: This delta reverts the nonce/`state` echo end to end: `startCallbackServer()` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:153-182) now resolves `callbackPromise` for any `GET /callback?code=…` with no check that the code belongs to this login, `github-auth.guard.ts:24` no longer stores a nonce, and `auth.controller.ts:127` no longer echoes one back. The port is guessable and any page in the user's browser can navigate to it (RFC 8252 §8.9), so the terminal can be silently pointed at another account's session. The deleted `packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts` was the only regression guard. Primary ownership is the security lens; raised here because the outcome is a wrong/overwritten persisted session (state corruption), and because the delta also removes the only test of that behaviour.

findings.summary: `login` labels every backend failure `UNAUTHORIZED`, contradicting the documented Error Matrix (5xx → SYSTEM) and the exit-code column
findings.evidence: `failFromBackend` is called with a hard-coded `code: 'UNAUTHORIZED'` fallback at login.ts:84, :101 and :120 regardless of status — the workspaces call at :118-123 even interpolates `HTTP ${wsRes.status}` into the message while still coding it `UNAUTHORIZED`, so a 500 from `/workspaces` is reported to an agent as an auth failure. docs/design/cli.md §10 (line 1117-1118) specifies `Backend 401/403 → exit 2, UNAUTHORIZED` and `Backend 5xx or network → exit 2, SYSTEM`; these paths exit 1 and never emit SYSTEM. findings.summary: Browser (non-CLI) GitHub login still sends no OAuth `state`, so the callback validates nothing — forced-login CSRF
findings.evidence: `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` only mints a state token when `mode === 'cli'` (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:59), and `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` only sets `opts.state` when `req.__cliStateToken` is present (github.strategy.ts:59-62). passport-oauth2 with no `state` option installs a NullStore, whose `verify` always succeeds, so a plain browser login sends no `state` to GitHub and `githubAuthCallback` reaches the web branch with `stateToken === undefined` (auth.controller.ts:119,145) and sets `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` cookies unconditionally. Attack: attacker starts the GitHub consent dance himself, captures the unredeemed `?code=…` from his own callback URL, and gets the victim to load `https://<backend>/auth/github/callback?code=<attacker code>` (image/iframe/link). The victim's browser is issued cookies for the ATTACKER's account, and everything the victim then creates lands in the attacker's workspace. This diff's own `rest-api.md` risk table records the gap as "Not mitigated" and defers it, and the CLI hardening does not close it — reporting it so the deferral is an explicit decision rather than an implicit one. Pre-existing, not introduced here.

findings.summary: The nonce and the PKCE challenge travel in one URL that the CLI prints to stderr and the backend logs on any 4xx — an observer of that single line defeats both "independent" bindings
findings.evidence: `login` builds `…/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>&code_challenge=<S256>` (login.ts:53-56) and prints it verbatim with `console.error('Opening browser: ' + oauthUrl)` (login.ts:57) — stderr an agent harness captures into logs, issue reports and shared transcripts. Backend-side, `customLogLevel` in app.module.ts:50 returns `warn` for any `statusCode >= 400`, and the `req` serializer logs the full `req.url` (app.module.ts:69) with no redaction of query params (redact covers only authorization/cookie/set-cookie, app.module.ts:77-84), so the new `BadRequestException('Invalid code_challenge')` path (github-auth.guard.ts:76) writes port+nonce+challenge to the production access log. An attacker who reads that one line inside the 30-second listen window replays the SAME nonce and the SAME `code_challenge` in his own `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim port>&nonce=<victim nonce>&code_challenge=<victim challenge>` request, consents as himself, and pushes the resulting redirect at `http://127.0.0.1:<victim port>/callback?code=ATTACKER&state=<victim nonce>`. The state echo matches, and `consumeCode` accepts because SHA256(victim verifier) equals the reused challenge (cli-auth.store.ts:127-130) — the victim's terminal is logged into the attacker's account. Both bindings derive from values shipped together in one observable string, so the independence claimed in docs/design/cli.md and rest-api.md does not hold against an observer of the authorization request. Mitigations worth considering: do not print the query string (print only a shortened/opaque handle, or a URL without `nonce`/`code_challenge` when a browser can be opened), and/or bind the code to the requesting session so a second authorization request reusing a live nonce is rejected.

findings.summary: `failFromBackend` relies solely on `process.exit` to stop the login flow; nothing returns, so if the exit is intercepted the very next line re-reads an already-consumed body
findings.evidence: `if (!exchangeRes.ok) { await failFromBackend(exchangeRes, name, {...}); }` (login.ts:82-87) — there is no `return`. `failFromBackend` (line 178) consumes the body with `await res.json()` and then calls `process.exit(1)`. TypeScript does NOT treat `await someFn()` returning `Promise<never>` as a control-flow terminator, so the compiler happily keeps `const tokens = (await exchangeRes.json())` (line 89) reachable. In any environment where `process.exit` does not actually terminate (a stubbed/patched exit, an `exitOverride`-style harness, or a future refactor that replaces the exit with a throwing helper), execution falls through and `exchangeRes.json()` throws `TypeError: Body is unusable`, masking the real backend reason the envelope was just built to surface. The same pattern repeats for `meRes` (line 99) and `wsRes` (line 118). An explicit `return` after each `failFromBackend` call would make the intent enforced rather than incidental.

findings.summary: New `/auth` log-redaction helper `logSafeUrl` has no test at all (and is unexported, so it cannot be tested)
findings.evidence: `logSafeUrl` implements a security-motivated behavior (replace the query string of any `/auth` URL with `?<redacted>`, keep the query elsewhere) with a non-trivial regex `/^\/auth(?:\/|$)/` and a non-string passthrough. There is no `packages/backend/src/app.module.spec.ts` (Glob over `packages/backend/src/**/*.spec.ts` lists none) and a repo-wide grep for `logSafeUrl` returns only app.module.ts:34/87 plus a prose mention in docs/design/rest-api.md:396. Nothing exercises the boundary cases the comment claims (`/authors?x=1` must NOT be redacted; `/auth` with no query; a non-string url). The function is also module-private, so a regression here is invisible to every lane.

findings.summary: The renamed `__cliStateToken` → `__oauthState` handoff from guard to strategy is not covered by any test
findings.evidence: `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` now reads `req.__oauthState` and copies it into `opts.state`; `github-auth.guard.ts:111,116` is the only writer. github.strategy.spec.ts only asserts endpoint URLs — it never calls `authenticate` or inspects `opts.state`. A grep for `__oauthState`/`__cliStateToken` across packages/backend finds matches only in the guard, the guard spec, the strategy source and a controller comment — no test asserts the strategy forwards it. If the two ever disagree (a half-applied rename), the authorization request would reach GitHub with no `state` at all (passport-oauth2's NullStore always verifies), i.e. no CSRF binding, and the whole backend suite would still be green.

findings.summary: Scope: two unrelated efforts are bundled in one change. (a) OAuth security hardening — CLI nonce echo, PKCE S256, browser double-submit `state` cookie, `/auth` access-log redaction — touching backend auth guard/controller/store and cli login; and (b) the CLI error-envelope refactor attributed to #661 — one-line envelopes, `command` attribution, shared `errorEnvelope`/`backendErrorEnvelope`, session-command conversion — touching ~20 CLI files. Only the `login` failure-reporting rewrite sits at their intersection. No originating issue accompanied this review, so I cannot map either half to an acceptance criterion; if the charter is one of the two, the other half is unrequested scope.

findings.summary: CLI OAuth `state` is not bound to the browser that started the flow, so an attacker who can bind a loopback port on the victim's machine can capture the victim's authorization code
findings.evidence:
The change adds a browser binding for the web flow (a `w.`-prefixed state whose other half is the `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie, github-auth.guard.ts:128-139, checked at auth.controller.ts:174-188) but the CLI branch (github-auth.guard.ts:105-111) mints a bare store-backed token with no cookie and no per-browser binding, and auth.controller.ts:190-194 accepts it from ANY browser.

Vector: (1) the attacker binds 127.0.0.1:P on a shared host / container / multi-user dev box the victim also uses; (2) the attacker calls `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=P&nonce=N&code_challenge=C` themselves and reads `state=S` straight out of their own 302 `Location` header — the endpoint is unauthenticated, so S is free; (3) the attacker phishes the victim with `https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize?client_id=…&state=S`; the victim (already having authorized the app) is silently redirected to `/auth/github/callback?code=<victim's GitHub code>&state=S`; (4) `verifyCallbackState` finds S in the CLI store and returns it, `findOrCreateUser` resolves to the **victim**, and auth.controller.ts:140-149 redirects the victim's browser to `http://127.0.0.1:P/callback?code=<code>&state=N` — the attacker's listener; (5) the attacker redeems the code at `POST /auth/cli/exchange` with the verifier V they chose in step 2 and receives the victim's access + refresh tokens.

The nonce echo does not help (the attacker picked N) and PKCE does not help (the attacker picked C and holds V). The `state` echo protects the CLI *from* injected codes; nothing protects the *server* from a CLI state replayed in an unrelated browser. The natural fix is to give the CLI state the same cookie half the web state now gets (or to require the CLI's own confirmation of the browser that started it).

findings.summary: The authorization URL carrying both login bindings (nonce + PKCE challenge) is printed to stderr on browser-open failure, which is exactly the headless/agent case; an observer of that log can hijack the pending login
findings.evidence:
`console.error(oauthUrl)` at login.ts:80 emits `…/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>&code_challenge=<challenge>`. The comment at login.ts:52-59 and docs/design/cli.md acknowledge that anyone who reads this URL can start their own login under the same nonce and challenge and push the resulting code at the port — and because the victim's CLI holds the matching verifier, it will happily redeem the attacker's code (cli-auth.store.ts:127-132 accepts it: the challenge matches). Result: the terminal is logged into the attacker's account and every subsequent `wafflebase` write lands in the attacker's workspace.

The mitigation chosen (print only when `open` fails) inverts against the CLI's stated audience: headless CI and agent harnesses are precisely where `open` fails and where stderr is captured verbatim into logs and issue reports. The window is the 5-minute state TTL. A binding that survives disclosure of the start URL — e.g. printing only a short user_code and having the CLI hold a secret it never puts on the URL (RFC 8628 device flow), or deriving the nonce from a value the CLI never transmits — would close it.

searchedFor: read packages/backend/src/main.ts for setGlobalPrefix / router options
grep for 'case sensitive' / router configuration in backend
findings.summary: `/auth` access-log redaction is case- and normalization-sensitive while Express routing is not, so login secrets can still land in the access log
findings.evidence: `logSafeUrl` gates on `/^\/auth(?:\/|$)/.test(path)` (app.module.ts:39), an exact, lowercase, literal prefix test on the raw `req.url`. Express's router defaults to `case sensitive routing: false`, so `GET /AUTH/github?mode=cli&nonce=…&code_challenge=…` and `GET /Auth/github/callback?code=…&state=…` are routed to `AuthController` exactly as the lowercase forms are, but neither matches the redaction regex — the full query string (the CLI's nonce and challenge outbound, GitHub's `code` and `state` inbound) is written verbatim to the access log, and the comment itself notes every 4xx on these routes logs at `warn`. Matching against the resolved route (or lowercasing / normalising `path` before the test) closes it. Impact if triggered is precisely the exposure the redaction was added to prevent — a replayable login parked in the log.

searchedFor: read docs/design/cli.md compatibility section in the diff
findings.summary: The server still accepts CLI logins with no nonce and no code_challenge, leaving RFC 8252 §8.9 code injection fully open for any client that does not opt in
findings.evidence: Both bindings are optional server-side: `boundedToken(req.query?.nonce, 1, MAX_NONCE_LENGTH)` (github-auth.guard.ts:108) yields `undefined` when absent, the controller then emits no `state` echo (auth.controller.ts:144-146), and `consumeCode` returns the userId for an unchallenged code presented bare (cli-auth.store.ts:122-123). Any CLI that does not send the parameters — including the previously shipped one, which by the docs' own compatibility statement must keep working — is redeemed with the exact pre-change semantics: an attacker who guesses the loopback port pushes `http://127.0.0.1:P/callback?code=<attacker's code>` and the old CLI exchanges it, logging the terminal into the attacker's account. The guard's own bounds are also asymmetric: a malformed `code_challenge` is a 400 (line 101-103) but a malformed/over-long `nonce` is silently dropped (line 108), producing an unbound login the client believes is bound. Consider making both mandatory for `mode=cli` (or gating the legacy path behind an explicit opt-in) once the CLI version floor allows it, and treating a present-but-malformed `nonce` the same way as a malformed challenge.

findings.summary: `opened = true` after `open()` resolves is not evidence a browser opened, so headless users never see the OAuth URL

searchedFor: Grep for a callback/error route in packages/frontend/src
findings.summary: Browser login page has no handling for the new 401 the callback can now return
findings.evidence: packages/frontend/src/components/login-form.tsx:27 is the only browser entry point into the OAuth flow (`to={`${VITE_BACKEND_API_URL}/auth/github`}`). Before this change `GET /auth/github/callback` could not fail for a normal user; it now throws `UnauthorizedException('Login session expired or invalid...')` (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:183 / :210) whenever the `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie is absent or stale. That cookie has `maxAge: 5 * 60 * 1000` (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:161), so a user who sits on GitHub's consent screen for more than five minutes — or who has cookies blocked for the backend origin, or who completes an in-flight login across a deploy — lands on a raw Nest JSON 401 page on the *backend* origin with no link back to the app. The frontend consumer was not updated to catch or recover from this new failure mode (no error route, no retry affordance). The fix likely belongs on the backend: redirect to `FRONTEND_URL` with an error query parameter instead of throwing, or on the frontend by adding a callback-error landing page.

findings.summary: `openBrowser`'s new async-error absorption is fully mocked away — no test can fail if it regresses
findings.evidence: The whole point of the new `openBrowser` helper is that `open()` resolves on spawn and the failure arrives later as an async `error` event on the child (`child?.on?.('error', () => {})`, login.ts:180), which unhandled kills the process. The only test file that drives `login` (`packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:15`) mocks the module wholesale: `vi.mock('open', () => ({ default: vi.fn(async () => undefined) }))`, so `child` is always `undefined` and the `.on('error')` registration is never exercised. There is no test anywhere that returns a child emitting `error`, nor one where the dynamic `import('open')` rejects. Deleting the `child?.on?.(...)` line leaves every test green.

findings.summary: backend.md — the canonical backend design doc — is left describing the old auth surface, so the repo now has two design docs that contradict each other on the same endpoints. The change updates cli.md and rest-api.md only, but backend.md's API Reference still documents `GET /auth/github` as plain "Initiates GitHub OAuth flow" with no `state`/cookie (line 103-105), `GET /auth/github/callback` as unconditionally upserting the user and setting cookies with no state validation (line 107-115), and `POST /auth/cli/exchange` as `Body: { code }` (line 146) with no `codeVerifier`. The cookie table (lines 312-313) lists only `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` and omits the new `wafflebase_oauth_state` (httpOnly, SameSite=Lax, path=/auth, 5 min), and the Observability section's redaction bullet (line 348-349) lists only header redaction, not the new `/auth` query-string redaction the `req` serializer now performs. CONTRIBUTING's design-doc discipline expects the canonical subsystem doc to be folded forward with an architecture/behavior change of this size.
findings.evidence: backend.md:103-115 (`/auth/github`, callback), :146 (`Body: { code }`), :312-313 (cookie table), :348-349 (redaction) vs app.module.ts:70 `logSafeUrl`, github-auth.guard.ts (state cookie), auth.dto.ts `codeVerifier`.

findings.summary: The CLI login URL — which carries the whole nonce + PKCE challenge pair — is handed to `open()`, i.e. placed in a child process's argv, where any local user can read it and defeat all three new loopback bindings
findings.evidence: `announceLoginUrl` (login.ts:199) goes to great lengths to keep the authorization URL off stderr because "anyone who reads it can start their own login against the same pair and push the resulting code at this port", and writes it 0600 when stderr is not a TTY. But `openBrowser` (login.ts:176-184) passes the same URL to `open(url)`, which spawns `xdg-open <url>` / `open <url>` / a powershell shim with the URL as a command-line argument. On Linux with the default `hidepid=0` /proc (and on macOS via `ps`), any other local user sees `mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>&code_challenge=<challenge>` in full. Attack: local attacker reads the URL from `ps`; opens `https://server/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim's port>&nonce=<victim's nonce>&code_challenge=<victim's challenge>` in their own browser and consents as themselves; the backend mints a code bound to the copied challenge and redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:<victim port>/callback?code=A&state=<victim nonce>` — the same loopback the victim's CLI is listening on. The CLI's `nonceMatches` (login.ts:331) passes because the nonce was copied, and `POST /auth/cli/exchange` succeeds because the victim's verifier hashes to the copied challenge (cli-auth.store.ts:136). The victim's terminal is now logged into the attacker's account and every subsequent `wafflebase` write lands in the attacker's workspace — exactly the RFC 8252 §8.9 injection this change claims to close, on the multi-user host the change's own docs put in scope (docs/design/cli.md 'Browser binding').

findings.summary: Anyone can start a `mode=cli` login pointing at an arbitrary loopback port; the new browser-binding cookie does not stop the start-URL variant of the phishing attack it is documented as closing
findings.evidence: `GET /auth/github` is unauthenticated and accepts `mode=cli&port=<any 1024-65535>&nonce=<attacker's>&code_challenge=<attacker's>` from any origin (github-auth.guard.ts:98-129). The browser-binding cookie only rules out an attacker *pre-minting* a state in their own browser and replaying the callback; it does nothing when the attacker simply gets the victim to click the crafted **start** URL — the victim's own browser then mints the cookie, passes `verifyCallbackState` (auth.controller.ts:190-200), and the server redirects the victim to `http://127.0.0.1:<attacker-chosen port>/callback?code=<victim's code>&state=<attacker's nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:145). Because the attacker chose the `code_challenge`, they hold the verifier, so PKCE does not protect the code either: an attacker with any listener on the victim's loopback (shared/multi-user host, or a malicious local helper) redeems the victim's code at `/auth/cli/exchange` and receives the victim's access + refresh tokens. The guard comment (github-auth.guard.ts:76-81) and the risk row in docs/design/rest-api.md:399 both assert the cookie closes 'an attacker mints a CLI state pointing at a loopback port they own and walks the victim through consent', which is only true for the callback-replay variant — a control that reads as covered but is not.

findings.summary: The browser-flow CSRF defense is an unsigned double-submit cookie with a `Domain`-settable name, so a sibling-subdomain cookie injection still yields forced-login CSRF
findings.evidence: `issueStateCookie` sets `wafflebase_oauth_state` with `httpOnly/sameSite=lax/path=/auth` but no integrity binding, no `__Host-`/`__Secure-` name prefix, and `secure` only when NODE_ENV==='production'. `verifyCallbackState` (auth.controller.ts:179-188) accepts any callback where the presented `w.<value>` equals the cookie value. An attacker who controls or XSSes any sibling subdomain (or, in a non-production deployment, an on-path attacker over plain HTTP) can set `wafflebase_oauth_state=X; Domain=.<site>; Path=/auth` in the victim's browser and then navigate the victim to `/auth/github/callback?code=<attacker's GitHub code>&state=w.X`. Both halves match, so the victim's browser is issued `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` for the attacker's account — the forced-login CSRF this change is meant to close. Signing/HMACing the cookie value against the state, or a `__Host-`-prefixed cookie, would remove the injection path.

findings.summary: `logSafeUrl` redacts only `/auth` query strings, so the share-link credential in `GET /documents/:id/file?token=<share token>` is still written to the access log verbatim
findings.evidence: The new serializer (app.module.ts:70) redacts a query string only when `isAuthPath` matches `^/auth(/|$)` (log-safe-url.ts:22). `packages/backend/src/document/document-file.controller.ts:40` accepts an anonymous share-link credential as `@Query('token')` and uses it in `assertCanRead` (line 49) to grant document read access. That request path is not under `/auth`, so pino logs `url: "/documents/<id>/file?token=<share-token>"` in full — and 4xx there logs at `warn`, so failed/expired attempts are captured too. Anyone who can read the access log (operator, log shipper, agent harness transcript) gains read access to the shared document. The redaction control is introduced as 'login secrets in access logs' but stops at one route prefix.

findings.summary: New user-facing login error banner (`?error=login_state` → mapped message, plus fallback) has no test at all
findings.evidence: login-form.tsx now reads `useSearchParams()` and renders a `role="alert"` div using ERROR_MESSAGES[error] ?? FALLBACK_ERROR. This is the only feedback a user gets when the OAuth callback refuses their login (the backend redirects to `/login?error=login_state`). Frontend has a running vitest lane with many component tests (e.g. packages/frontend/src/components/__tests__/datasource-dialog.test.tsx, app/files/__tests__/generic-file-view.test.tsx), but there is no test file for login-form or the login page — a regression that dropped the banner or the fallback mapping would ship silently.

findings.summary: Session/refresh cookie `Secure` flag is now derived from `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`'s scheme, so a misconfigured `http://` callback on a TLS-fronted deployment silently drops `Secure` from the session token
findings.evidence: `baseCookieOptions()` changed from `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'` to `secure: secureCookies(this.configService)` (auth.controller.ts:528). `secureCookies` (github-auth.guard.ts:91-98) returns `false` for *any* `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` starting with `http://`, and that branch is checked before the `NODE_ENV==='production'` fallback. Previously a production deployment always got `Secure` session/refresh cookies regardless of that variable. Now a deployment that terminates TLS at a proxy and leaves `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL=http://...` (the exact spelling the self-hosting guide prints, packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:121) serves `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` without `Secure` on an https site — the JWT then rides any plaintext request to the origin and is trivially stolen by a network attacker or a downgrade link. The reasoning in the comment (a Secure cookie on an http origin is dropped) is sound for a genuinely-http origin, but the predicate reads a config string, not the actual serving scheme, so one wrong env value silently removes a transport control from the session cookie rather than only from the 5-minute login cookie. Consider keeping `secure: true` whenever `NODE_ENV==='production'` OR the callback is https, and only relaxing for loopback.
